content:
Knee osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis in the UK. It causes knee pain that is worse with activity, short-lived stiffness, and sometimes swelling and grinding. Exercise to strengthen the leg muscles is the most important treatment, alongside weight loss if needed and simple pain relief. Knee replacement is considered when symptoms seriously affect your life despite these.

Symptoms

  • pain in the knee, often worse with walking, stairs or standing up
  • stiffness after resting or first thing in the morning, usually lasting less than 30 minutes
  • swelling, which can come and go
  • grinding or crunching
  • the knee feeling weak or giving way
  • reduced bending or straightening

Symptoms often go through better and worse periods.

Related reading: Sarcopenia and knee osteoarthritis: the frailty overlap (UK), Best Knee Exercises for Arthritis, Can You Prevent Knee Osteoarthritis? UK Evidence Review

Risk factors

  • being over 45
  • being overweight
  • previous knee injury, such as a torn ligament or cartilage
  • jobs involving lots of kneeling or squatting
  • weak thigh muscles
  • family history
  • being female

Diagnosis

NICE (NG226) says knee osteoarthritis can be diagnosed without X-rays in people over 45 with activity-related joint pain and morning stiffness of no more than 30 minutes. X-ray findings do not always match symptoms. Your GP may arrange tests if the picture is unusual, for example if the knee is hot and swollen or you have symptoms in several joints.

Exercise: the core treatment

NICE recommends therapeutic exercise tailored to each person. For the knee this includes:

  • strengthening: sit to stand, straight-leg raises, step-ups, mini squats holding the worktop
  • aerobic activity: walking, cycling, swimming or water exercise
  • flexibility: gentle stretches for the thigh and calf muscles

Some discomfort during exercise is normal and does not mean you are causing damage. If pain is still increased the next day, reduce the amount a little but keep going. Benefits build over weeks.

Many areas offer NHS group programmes, such as ESCAPE-pain, or self-referral to physiotherapy.

Weight management

If you are overweight, losing weight reduces the load on your knees and can noticeably ease pain. Your GP can refer you to local weight management services.

Pain relief

  • topical NSAID gels are recommended by NICE as a first option for knee osteoarthritis
  • oral NSAIDs may be considered for a short time at the lowest effective dose, with stomach protection if needed
  • paracetamol and weak opioids are not routinely recommended by NICE for osteoarthritis unless used occasionally and short-term

Ask your pharmacist or GP what suits you.

Other things that may help

  • heat or cold packs
  • supportive, cushioned footwear
  • a walking stick, held in the hand opposite the painful knee
  • knee supports or braces for some people
  • TENS machines, which some people find useful

Injections

Steroid injections may give short-term relief during a bad flare and can help you exercise. NICE does not recommend hyaluronic acid injections.

What is not recommended

NICE does not recommend glucosamine or chondroitin, acupuncture, or arthroscopic "washout" surgery for knee osteoarthritis.

Knee replacement

Joint replacement may be considered if pain, stiffness and reduced function substantially affect your quality of life despite non-surgical treatment. Age, weight and smoking should not be barriers to referral on their own, though your surgeon will discuss how they affect risks. Partial knee replacement is an option for some people.

Living with knee osteoarthritis

Keep active, pace demanding tasks, use stair rails and raise low chairs. Many people find their symptoms stay stable or improve with regular exercise and do not need surgery.

Questions to ask your GP or physiotherapist

  • Which exercises are best for my knee, and how many should I do?
  • Is there a group exercise programme near me?
  • Which pain relief is safest for me?
  • At what point should we talk about surgery?

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
